opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest limitation is that an intervention tells you what *can* happen in the model, not necessarily what *does* happen when it's running normally.

When you intervene, say you patch an activation, ablate a component, or steer along some direction, you're pushing the model into a state it might never visit on its own. If the output changes the way your hypothesis predicts, that's real evidence. But the model is a very high-dimensional, very flexible system, and it can often be pushed into the behavior you're looking for through many different routes. So a successful intervention shows that your proposed mechanism is *sufficient* to produce the behavior. It doesn't show it's the mechanism the model actually uses.

A few concrete versions of this problem come up a lot:

- **Off-distribution activations.** Zero-ablation or large steering vectors produce internal states that are unlike anything the model saw in training. The downstream effects might reflect the model breaking in strange ways rather than revealing the function of the component.
- **Redundancy and self-repair.** You knock out a component and nothing changes, so you conclude it doesn't matter. In fact other parts of the network compensated. The reverse also happens: you get a big effect and overestimate how central something is.
- **Expressivity of the intervention.** This one I think about a lot. If your intervention method is powerful enough, like a learned rotation or a nonlinear map applied to the activations, you can make almost any hypothesis "work." At that point you're partly measuring what your intervention can do, not what the model encodes. So you need to constrain the intervention or compare it against good baselines. Otherwise "I found a feature that controls X" can be close to vacuous.
- **Choice of counterfactuals.** Interchange-style interventions depend heavily on which input pairs you pick. A mechanism can look clean on a carefully chosen dataset and fall apart on a broader one.

None of that means interventions aren't useful. They're one of the few tools we have that give causal rather than merely correlational evidence, and that matters a lot. But a lot of the rigor in this area comes down to being honest about that gap. You should ask whether your intervention keeps the model in a realistic regime, whether a simpler or random baseline would do just as well, and whether your hypothesis predicts behavior on inputs you didn't tune on. If you skip those checks, it's easy to tell a very convincing story that the model isn't actually following.

r001.rationale: The response recommends constraining interventions and testing broader inputs, but does not identify restricting investigations to narrowly scoped problems as a limitation.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss designing an intervention experiment to determine whether a model is considering lying to its user.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose automating hypothesis-driven investigations with a language-model agent or intervention tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core limitation is that when you intervene on a model, you're not just testing your hypothesis about what the model is doing, you're also pushing it into a state it may never actually occupy. So you have to be careful about what your result means.

Take a concrete example. Say I have a hypothesis that some direction in the residual stream encodes "the subject is in France." The natural thing to do is patch that direction, or ablate it, and see if the model's output changes the way I'd predict. And often it does, which feels like strong evidence. But the model has a lot of redundancy and a lot of freedom to compensate. If I ablate something and the behavior survives, that doesn't mean the feature wasn't being used. It might just mean there's a backup pathway that only turns on when I break the primary one. Conversely, if I overwrite a direction with a big enough vector, I can get almost any behavior out of the model, and that tells me more about what the model can be forced to do than about what it does normally.

So intervention gives you causal evidence, which is genuinely better than correlational probing, but it's causal evidence about a distribution the model was never trained on. The off-distribution problem cuts both ways. You can get false negatives from compensation and false positives from steering too hard.

The other issue is that the hypothesis space you can test is bounded by the interventions you know how to make. If the true mechanism is something I don't have a clean handle for, like a nonlinear combination of features or something spread across many layers, I'll end up testing a simplified version of it and possibly confirming a story that's wrong in the details. Interventions are great for checking "is this component necessary or sufficient for this behavior," but that's a narrower question than "what is the model actually computing."

The way I think about it is that intervention is a tool for ruling things out and establishing lower bounds on involvement, not for proving you've found the whole mechanism. You want to pair it with things that constrain the hypothesis more tightly, like checking that the intervention effect is tightly localized and that it scales the way you'd expect, or comparing against what the model does on natural inputs where the variable actually varies.

astra-6.text: The main limitation is that an intervention can tell you that something matters without telling you exactly what it does. Suppose you think a particular component implements some behavior, and you knock it out and the behavior disappears. That’s evidence that the component is important, but it doesn’t necessarily establish your proposed mechanism. You might have disrupted something else the model needs, or pushed it into a state it never encounters naturally. So the challenge is making the intervention specific enough to distinguish your hypothesis from other explanations, rather than just showing that you can break the model.

r001.rationale: The response says interventions should be specific enough to distinguish hypotheses, but does not identify restricting investigations to narrowly scoped problems as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether an AI model is considering lying to its user or the difficulty of designing an intervention to determine that.

r003.rationale: It proposes no automation using a language-model agent or model-intervention tools.

sol-6.1.text: The main limitation is that an intervention can tell you that something matters without telling you exactly what it does. If I remove a component and the model gets worse, that’s evidence the component was important, but it doesn’t uniquely establish my explanation of its role. I might also have pushed the model into an unusual state, where its behavior no longer reflects how it normally works. So interventions are useful causal evidence, but you need controls and multiple complementary experiments to distinguish your hypothesis from other explanations.
